Her roommate Kavitha read it. "Where's this from? There's no name, no date, no news link."
"It doesn't matter. Everyone's sending it. You don't want to warn people?"
"I do. But I want it to be true first."
Usha felt a flash of irritation. How could Kavitha be so cold about something this serious? She didn't answer and sent it to her mother too.

Last monsoon I forwarded a message I still think about. It said that sleeping near a phone charger could cause brain problems, and to "share with everyone you love."
I'd seen it from Mamma, from my college group, from a neighbour. Everywhere. By the fourth time, it just felt true. I forwarded it to thirty people.
My friend Uday replied, "Francis, is there a source?" I was annoyed. I actually thought, why does he always have to be so cold? Can't he just care?
Later he sent me a link from a health ministry page saying there was no such evidence. I felt my face go hot.
What I learned: seeing something ten times doesn't make it true. It just makes it familiar. And Uday wasn't cold. He was the only one checking.

Nandini had been the nurse at the primary school for two years. On Monday, a TV channel showed a story about a child in another state who was bitten by a rare venomous spider in a school garden.
By Wednesday, parents were at the gate demanding the garden be closed. Sonali, the principal, agreed and had it locked. Some parents stopped sending children to outdoor PE altogether.
Nandini watched it all with a sinking feeling. In two years she had treated zero spider bites. She had treated forty scraped knees from the broken tiles near the staircase, and three children hit by speeding bikes at the school gate, where there was still no crossing guard.

Subject: About the lift ban
Dear Sahil,
As RWA president you've been flooded with messages, so I'll keep this short.
After the news video of a lift falling in another city, our building voted to stop using lifts. Now Mr Kulkarni, who's eighty-two, is climbing seven floors with his cane, and the Deshpandes carry their baby up and down every day.
I understand the fear. That video was terrifying. But our lifts were inspected last month and passed.
What worries me more: the stair lights on floors three and five have been broken for weeks, and the stairs are wet from the leak. More of us will slip on those stairs than will ever be in a lift accident.
Can we fix the lights and talk about this calmly on Sunday?
Nikita

Saurabh, beta, your phone keeps buzzing with that scary kidney-theft message? Let your Jaya Bua tell you what I did at your age.
When I was twenty-five, a message went round that a gang was kidnapping people at railway stations. Your Dadi forwarded it to me six times, with crying faces. My hands shook reading it.
But I sat down and traced it. I searched the first line. It came from a blog with no name. I checked the police website and the newspaper; nothing. I asked myself, how often does this actually happen here? I couldn't find a single real case.
So I didn't forward it. I called your Dadi and said gently, "Ma, I know it's scary. I checked, and I couldn't find it anywhere real. Let's not send it further." She was quiet, then said, "Okay."
